s1.syndrome_frame: Sudden onset of bilateral vision loss following trauma
salient_findings: Normal anterior and posterior segment examinations
Normal visual evoked potentials and electroretinography
key_facts: 30-year-old man with no prior medical or psychiatric history
Sudden onset of bilateral vision loss after a fall
Fall was approximately 3 meters from a pickup truck
Patient had a concussion and a superficial scalp laceration
Initial visual acuity was counting fingers bilaterally
Visual acuity decreased to no light perception in both eyes the following day
Systemic and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable
Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15
Relative afferent pupillary defect testing, fogging test, and menace reflex were all normal
Noncontrast computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no abnormalities

shortlist.label: Traumatic optic neuropathy
shortlist.why_kept: Direct trauma to the optic nerve from the fall

shortlist.label: Conversion disorder
shortlist.why_kept: Sudden onset of bilateral vision loss without clear organic cause

shortlist.label: Bilateral optic neuritis
shortlist.why_kept: Inflammation of the optic nerve could explain vision loss

shortlist.label: Bilateral ischemic optic neuropathy
shortlist.why_kept: Possible compromise of blood supply to the optic nerves

shortlist.label: Cortical blindness
shortlist.why_kept: Possible damage to the visual cortex from the concussion

raw.rationale: Normal findings on thorough ophthalmologic and neurologic examinations, including normal visual evoked potentials and electroretinography, suggest a non-organic cause of vision loss, which is consistent with conversion disorder, especially given the psychological stress of a recent traumatic event.

rejected.label: Traumatic optic neuropathy
rejected.why: Normal visual evoked potentials and lack of other optic nerve damage signs make this less likely

rejected.label: Bilateral optic neuritis
rejected.why: Normal findings on ophthalmologic examinations, including no relative afferent pupillary defect, argue against this diagnosis

rejected.label: Bilateral ischemic optic neuropathy
rejected.why: Absence of risk factors and normal optic disc appearance make this diagnosis unlikely

rejected.label: Cortical blindness
rejected.why: Normal neuroimaging and lack of other neurologic deficits make this diagnosis unlikely
